Silicon nitride strings and membranes from 30 to 340~nm thickness follow the predicted volume scaling, the predicted $σ_0^{-2}$ dilution across resonators and within stress-engineered strings, and the predicted thickness dependence, which places noise-active two-level systems in the volume and at the surfaces of the resonators, all at the absolute level set by the independently measured intrinsic loss. The same relation accounts for published data between 78 and 296~K; below 78~K, the loss measured at the resonance no longer represents the loss probed by the noise, marking the limit of the structural-damping assumption. Dissipation dilution therefore lowers the $1/f$ floor, and the longest useful integration time of a resonant sensor is set by its prestress, volume, temperature, and intrinsic loss angle.

papers.title: Interlayer Registry Controls Polar Topology in Twisted Bilayer h-BN
papers.summary: Twisting van der Waals bilayers creates a moir'e stacking field with periodically varying local interlayer registry, enabling spatially patterned polarization. However, a systematic understanding of how this registry-controlled polar topology evolves with twist angle, temperature, and mechanical strain is still lacking. Here, using first-principles-trained deep-potential molecular dynamics simulations, we show that spatially varying interlayer registry governs the polarization texture and can be directly tuned by twist and relative layer deformation. As the twist angle decreases, the moir'e polarization texture evolves from compact, nearly circular vortex-like patterns to extended triangular AB/BA domains. This crossover arises from enhanced lattice relaxation at small twist angles, which expands low-energy, oppositely polarized AB/BA regions and confines in-plane polarization mainly to domain boundaries. Despite this reconstruction, the local in-plane winding remains tied to interlayer registry and persists up to 1000 K, indicating robust topology against thermal fluctuations. We further show that the mechanical response is dictated by whether deformation changes the relative registry: homogeneous deformation of both layers produces only weak distortions, whereas layer-selective deformation strongly reconstructs the moiré polarization texture. A mismatch-matrix registry-mapping model is developed to capture this response, explaining deformation-induced changes in vortex radii at larger twist angles and triangular-domain geometry at smaller twist angles. These results identify interlayer registry as the central control parameter for forming and tuning moir'e polar topology in twisted bilayer h-BN.

papers.title: Enhancing Quasi-Two-Dimensional Electronic Structure in Bi2O2Se via Chlorine Substitution
papers.summary: Bismuth oxyselenide (Bi2O2Se) has emerged as a leading semiconductor candidate for next-generation electronics and quantum phenomena research. However, its strong ionic interlayer bonding of Se layers fundamentally restricts the full potential of this otherwise promising quasi-two-dimensional (2D) material. In this work, we demonstrate chlorine substitution as an effective strategy to introduce van der Waals gaps and modify the electronic structure of the system. Through comprehensive transport and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) measurements on Bi6O6Se2Cl2 single crystal, an optimal Cl-doping compound, we show that the key electronic features, including indirect band gap, high electron mobility, and carrier effective mass, are well preserved, while the 2D character of the system is sufficiently enhanced. First-principles calculations attribute this selective tunability to the unique spatial separation between conductive Bi-O layers and dopant Se/Cl layers, which enables independent optimization of interlayer coupling and intralayer transport. Remarkably, our theoretical calculations combined with experimental observations project a broad bandgap engineering across a wide range (0.8 ~ 3.5 eV) within the Bi2O2Se system. Our findings not only expand the application potential of Bi2O2Se-based materials in optoelectronics, nanoelectronics, and fundamental research but also highlight spatial decoupling as a viable strategy for modifying detailed electronic structure of quasi-2D quantum systems.

papers.title: Single anyons and anyon binding in a quantum Hall dot
papers.summary: Anyons are particles with quantized fractional statistics. In theory, a single anyon can be stabilized as a localized fractional charge within the bulk of a topologically ordered two-dimensional insulator. However, experiments to date have focused on probing anyons in structures in which many anyonic excitations coexist and interact. Here, we demonstrate the trapping of a single anyon in a device consisting of a graphene-based quantum point contact with an embedded tunable quantum Hall dot. Benchmarking our device at v = 1, we demonstrate backscattering between Fermi liquid edge states mediated by the whole-electron Coulomb blockade of the dot. The cleanliness and control available in our device allow depletion of the dot to the last quasihole, and we observe spin blockade for transitions to the opposite-spin Landau level. At v = 1/3 and 2/3, we observe backscattering resonances with three times the frequency, consistent with resonant transmission of e/3 charges via a single anyon transistor. We demonstrate controlled depletion to the last quasiparticle to form a single anyon quantum dot. Tracing the charge addition spectrum for quasiparticle number Nqp = 1-5, we observe highly irregular addition energies, consistent with DMRG modeling showing a complex orbital shell-filling behavior. At higher Nqp = 10-20, the addition energies show a striking pattern: quasiholes at 1/3 (and quasiparticles at 2/3) show a regular addition spectrum while quasiparticles at 1/3 (and quasiholes at 2/3) do not. We trace the origin of this irregularity to an attractive component of the inter-anyon interaction: by experimentally tuning the confining energy, we observe complete suppression of alternating charge sectors, after which the dot charges in increments of twice the fundamental charge. This observation indicates the emergence of an anyon binding energy as large as the charging energy.

papers.title: Dark state preparation in a zero-field-split molecular triplet
papers.summary: We propose a protocol to prepare and probe dark states in a single-molecule electron spin resonance based on atomic force microscopy (ESR-AFM), thus extending existing techniques developed to address Rabi oscillations. To this end, we simulate in analogy to atomic physics the coherent manipulation of a three-level system in the V-configuration using a multifrequency magnetic field. More specifically, we consider a neutral molecule with a zero-field-split (ZFS) first excited triplet and analyze within a pump-probe scheme the dynamics of the total triplet population. In the triplet subspace, the dark state is a coherent superposition formed by two ZFS states which does not evolve in time despite a continuous resonant driving towards the third one. We characterize the properties of this state comparing it to its fully incoherent counterpart. Within a density-matrix formalism for open systems, we then compute the expected dark state signatures both for ideal scenarios and for the realistic parameterization of ESR-AFM on pentacene.

papers.title: Altermagnetic Ground States on the Ammann--Beenker Tiling
papers.summary: We identify exact altermagnetic ground states of a classical Heisenberg model on a quasicrystal. Considering the Ammann--Beenker tiling as an example, we determine the ground states by exploiting the parity structure of its parent four-dimensional hypercubic lattice. The ground state hosts coplanar altermagnetic order characterized by the preserved spin-group symmetry $[C_{2x}\parallel C_{8z}]$. Without translational symmetry, the momentum-space spin splitting that usually identifies altermagnets is not directly accessible. We instead couple the spins to itinerant electrons and show spin-resolved transport with $g$-wave symmetry, confirming the altermagnetic nature in a nonperiodic system. Our results establish a geometric route to altermagnetic order in quasicrystals, connecting exact magnetic ground states to their spin-resolved transport signatures.

papers.title: Observation of stacked vortex structure with number controllable Majorana zero mode in Bi$_{2}$Te$_{3}$/FeTe heterojunction
papers.summary: Creation and control of Majorana zero modes (MZMs) in solid devices is the key challenge in realizing fault tolerant topological quantum computation. Here we report spectroscopic evidence for number controllable MZMs in stoichiometric one quintuple layer Bi$_{2}$Te$_{3}$/FeTe heterostructures, together with the observation of stacked vortices in superconducting islands. Low temperature scanning tunnelling microscopy and spectroscopy reveal a long period moire superlattice arising from lattice mismatch, which induces nanoscale modulation of superconducting gaps. Magnetic vortices exhibit a stacked core structure with two layer derived bound state branches: a dispersive branch evolving into an X-shaped pattern away from the vortex center, and a quantum-limit branch characterized by a spatially unsplit MZMs together with discrete integer quantized Caroli-de Gennes-Matricon states. Notably, MZMs are observed in all measured vortices, and their number can be tuned by magnetic field and the size of Bi$_{2}$Te$_{3}$ islands. These results establish stoichiometric 1QL-Bi$_{2}$Te$_{3}$/FeTe as a patterned superconducting interface that enables isolated and few-vortex Majorana configurations, providing a controlled platform for fuse MZMs.

papers.title: Imaging the topological sign of a Dirac mass with spin-polarized tunneling
papers.summary: A Dirac mass is characterized not only by its magnitude but also by its sign, which influences the Berry curvature, Hall response, and the propagation direction of chiral boundary modes. However, local spectroscopy of magnetic topological surfaces has so far accessed only the gap magnitude $|M|$. Here we show how the topological sign of $M$ can be determined locally. We first establish the sign information that spin-resolved tunneling can access and the reference required to obtain an absolute Hall sign. Although spin--orbital entanglement generally obscures the relation between measured spin and Dirac pseudospin, crystalline rotation symmetry alleviates this ambiguity at the band edge. On a $C_3$ axis, an axial tip couples to a fully spin-polarized state whose tunneling asymmetry directly reveals the sign of the occupied-band Berry curvature, independent of orbital composition. We further show that the zeroth Landau level provides an independent mass-sign measurement with an unpolarized tip, while opposite domains and their chiral domain-wall modes provide self-consistency checks. These results pave the way for imaging the locations where the topological character changes within a material, rather than merely identifying where a spectral gap appears.

papers.title: Progress in Cavitated Front Gridline Ag Paste for PERC Solar Cell Architecture
papers.summary: This paper reports on the progress made with the cavitated silver paste on passivated emitter rear contact cells (PERC) to reduce the series resistance. Thus, electrical and microscopy characterizations are used to examine these resistive losses. Fifteen 252 cm2 PERC cells were fabricated for this assessment. Under standard test conditions, these cells achieved a mean conversion efficiency of 21.87% and a maximum of 22.07%. The mean measured fill factor was 79.98%, compared with a pseudo-fill factor of 83.60%, giving a mean deficit of 3.62 percentage points. Fill factor decreased with increasing area-normalized series resistance, which ranged from 0.53 to 0.83 ohm-cm2, while open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current remained unvaried. These electrical trends support resistive current extraction as the principal contributor to fill-factor variation. Electroluminescence imaging revealed localized emission nonuniformity. Cross-sectional scanning transmission electron microscopy showed variation in the glass interfacial layer, while scanning electron microscopy identified micrometer and sub micrometer silver particles. Conductive atomic force microscopy after sequential removal of the bulk metal and glass revealed spatially heterogeneous current response. These observations are consistent with nonuniform electrical access at the contact, where restricted conducting pathways may concentrate on current and increase local voltage drops. The combined characterization identifies interfacial heterogeneity and the connectivity of conducting pathways as priorities for understanding and reducing extraction losses in cavitated silver metallization.

papers.title: Skyrmion gears: translation-to-rotation conversion of skyrmion clusters along periodic substrates
papers.summary: We investigate how the translational motion of a compact skyrmion cluster can be converted into collective rotation through interactions with a periodic obstacle substrate. Using an effective particle model, we consider a seven-skyrmion cluster driven along a one-dimensional array of repulsive obstacle sites. For suitable obstacle spacings and interaction strengths, repeated interactions with the substrate produce coherent clockwise or counterclockwise rotation, giving rise to gear-like cluster dynamics. We characterize these states using the translational velocity, Hall angle, angular velocity, structural deformation, and a dimensionless gear ratio that relates cluster rotation to motion over the substrate periodicity. Dynamical phase diagrams identify rotating, nonrotating, wall-guided, transverse, and deformed regimes. We further show that coherent rotation persists in the overdamped limit, demonstrating that the conversion mechanism does not require an intrinsic Magnus force and may therefore extend to other driven cluster systems, including colloidal assemblies. These results provide a simple route for controlling collective rotation through structured substrates.

papers.title: High-mobility spin transport mediated by indirect excitons in a van der Waals heterostructure
papers.summary: Efficient spin transport with high spin mobility is of both fundamental and practical significance for spintronics. Spin can be transferred by moving particles. However, particle scattering limits spin transfer and prevents high spin mobilities. In this work, we study the kinetics of spin transport mediated by a quantum system of indirect excitons (IXs) in a van der Waals heterostructure composed of atomically thin transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs). This spin transfer mechanism allows for the realization of efficient spin transport characterized by a high spin mobility reaching 10$^5$ cm$^2$/(eV$\cdot$s), which is orders of magnitude higher than that achieved via standard diffusive spin transport in TMD materials. The suppression of IX scattering enables high-mobility spin transport.

papers.title: Measuring higher-order bulk topology in a programmable quantum simulator
papers.summary: Topological insulators lie outside the standard Landau paradigm: Instead of being characterized by local order parameters and spontaneous symmetry breaking, their defining properties are encoded in the global structure of their quantum states and manifested as robust boundary states. Crystalline higher-order topological insulators can extend this principle by hosting localized corner modes in two and higher dimensions. Although these boundary modes can be detected spectroscopically through the local density of states, determining the underlying bulk topology, for example through nested Wilson loops, remains an outstanding experimental challenge. Here we use up to 728 qubits in a superconducting analogue-digital quantum simulator to realize and probe a hierarchy of one-, two-, and three-dimensional topological insulators governed by effective tight-binding Hamiltonians. By reconstructing complex propagators from real-space measurements, we obtain complementary boundary and bulk characterizations: local densities of states reveal localized boundary modes, whereas experimentally reconstructed band projectors yield bulk topological invariants, culminating in a three-dimensional octupole moment extracted through third nested Wilson loops. These results establish a route to realizing, characterizing, and manipulating topologically protected states in programmable three-dimensional quantum matter.

papers.title: Eigenstate transitions and critical transport in 3D Aubry-André model
papers.summary: We numerically study spectral and wave-function properties, as well as time evolution, in finite-size commensurate approximations of the 3D Aubry-André model. We explicitly show, through scaling analysis, the existence of two critical points. One of the critical points is a localization-delocalization transition in real-space, similar to the critical point in the 3D Anderson model. The other is a localization-delocalization transition in a dual momentum space, which does not have any analog in the 3D Anderson model. We estimate their values from spectral measures, such as the gap ratio and the spectral form factor, as well as from wave-function measures, such as the inverse participation ratio and the participation entropy. Additionally, we demonstrate that both critical points exhibit hallmarks of critical points between quantum ergodicity and localization. First, the eigenstates and the eigenspectrum at the critical point fulfill the mutual universal relation between the eigenspectrum compressibility $χ$ and the eigenstate fractal dimension $d^{(1)}$ [S. Jiricek et al., Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci. 123, e2518027123 (2026)]. Second, the dynamics of the wave packet at the critical point is governed by the critical dynamical exponent $z$, characterized by the spectral fractal dimension and the dimensionality of the lattice [M. Hopjan and L. Vidmar, Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 060401 (2025)]. Thus, similarly to the 3D Anderson model, the critical dynamical exponent is sub-diffusive with the value of $z=3$.

papers.title: Investigation on Thermal Stability of Epi-GeSn Directly on Si (001)
papers.summary: In this paper we investigate the structural properties and thermal stability of metastable Ge1-xSnx epilayers (~4.5 at.% Sn) grown directly on Si(001) substrates by high-resolution X-ray diffraction (HRXRD) and Raman spectroscopy. Our results demonstrate that both 70 and 140 nm films are fully relaxed, with the thicker film exhibiting a small tensile strain (+0.09%). The thermal stability of the heterostructures was evaluated up to 813 K using temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy and scanning electron microscopy. The surface-weighted Raman response (532 nm excitation) and surface morphology of the 70 nm film remain highly stable. In contrast, the 140 nm film undergoes severe degradation, characterized by significant attenuation and broadening of the Ge-Ge longitudinal optical phonon mode, alongside enhanced surface Sn segregation. These findings demonstrate that the thermal stability of direct GeSn/Si heterostructures is governed by the initial defect structure established during epitaxial growth, providing key design rules for understanding the fabrication of GeSn-based optoelectronic devices.

papers.title: Spiral Edge States in Topological 2D Sb2Te3 Crystals
papers.summary: This work explores the edge state conduction properties of twinned and spiraled, 2D Sb2Te3 topological insulator crystals. We show the structure supports spatially continuous edge states within two spiral and knotted edge conduction channels. The channels are connected through a topological defect. This geometry introduces boundary conditions into the 2D crystal that modifies the edge state dispersion. Using a combination of low loss Electron Energy Loss Spectroscopy, Magnetic Force Microscopy and traditional carrier transport measurements we identify a distinct excitation at 0.155 eV in the spiral that seems to be related to two isolated states within the gap. This state is localized to the crystal edges. The modification of edge state bands using manipulation of a systems quantum geometry may open new avenues for the use of 2D topological systems.

papers.title: Partitioning the magnetization raises the stability limit of ferromagnetic colloids
papers.summary: Magnetic actuation scales with a particle's magnetic moment, yet practical colloidal suspensions remain superparamagnetic or weakly magnetized, a permanent dipole drives a near contact attraction growing as the square of the moment, binding particles irreversibly. Here we show that this constraint depends not only on how much magnetic material a particle carries, but on where it sits. Partitioning a fixed moment M into N internal elements leaves the far field interaction, and every actuation force, unchanged while suppressing the near-field pair energy by 1/N. As we show in our experiments across 57 samples and three geometries, stability collapses onto a single $\sim M^{2}/N$ boundary, raising the accessible dipolar energy scale nearly 150-fold. A liquid-phase analogue of magnetic force microscopy images the engineered energy landscape directly. The resulting colloids outrun size-matched superparamagnetic beads in weak fields far from a magnetic source, suggesting their applicability in hard to reach places. Together, these results open a new operating regime for colloidal manipulation, with impactful implications in microfluidics and drug delivery.

papers.title: Emergence of quantum transport in SnTe films upon structural refinement
papers.summary: Topological crystalline insulators are distinguished from the conventional Z2 topological insulators by crystalline symmetry protection of the surface states. Quantitative characterization of these states requires magneto-transport measurements from which the phase coherence length and number of independent coherent channels can be extracted. Here we report such measurements on textured thin films of SnTe grown on Bi2Te3 buffered c-plane sapphire (Al2O3) by pulsed laser ablation. A post deposition annealing protocol was implemented to control the crystallographic texture, which reveals improved crystallinity and enhanced epitaxial alignment along the [111] direction in films annealed at elevated temperatures. The higher carrier density and lower resistivity seen in films annealed at 100 oC are suggestive of Sn vacancies which act as native acceptor defects, while films annealed at 200 oC approach the 1:1 stoichiometry. The magnetoresistance of all samples at T < 10 K characterized by a cusp centered around zero-field is suggestive of weak antilocalization and interpreted in the framework of the Hikami-Larkin-Nagaoka theory in the strong spin-orbit coupling limit. At T > 20 K, the MR is small and positive, and deviates from conventional Kohler scaling. An approximate collapse of the MR curves between 50 and 250 K is obtained using an empirical temperature-dependent scaling factor, indicating that changes in the Hall-derived carrier density alone cannot account for the observed scaling behavior. These results demonstrate that post growth annealing strongly influences the interplay between stoichiometry, crystallinity, and coherent transport in SnTe thin films.

papers.title: Confined Phase Transition Infiltration Coupled With In Situ Pore Sealing: Constructing Hard Carbon Rich in Closed Pore for Plateau‐Capacity‐Dominated Sodium Storage
papers.summary: Biomass‐derived hard carbon (HC) is a promising candidate for anode materials in sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs). However, abundant open pores generated during activation process often lead to severe proliferation of the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) and irreversible Na + consumption, severely compromising the initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE) and low‐voltage plateau capacity. This work proposes a synergistic strategy of confined phase transition infiltration and in situ pore sealing, using waste green tea as a precursor to construct a HC anode dominated by plateau capacity. Low dose of ZnCl 2 induces controllable hydrolysis and aromatization of cellulose and generate nanoscale open pores. These pores act as confined microreactors, inducing an in situ chemical vapor deposition like carbon growth that effectively “stitching” the open voids into solvent sieving closed pores. Consequently, it delivers a remarkable ICE of 79.1%, a high reversible capacity of 342.3 mAh g −1 at 0.1 A g −1 , and robust cycling stability (86.2% retention after 1000 cycles at 1.0 A g −1 ). In‐/ex situ analysis reveals that its reversible sodium storage mechanism encompasses a triple synergy of defect adsorption, interlayer intercalation, and closed pore filling with quasi metallic sodium clusters. The confined pore sealing engineering strategy provides a robust paradigm for designing high‐performance HC anodes.

papers.title: Brewing better batteries: transforming brewed coffee powder into lithium-ion anodes
papers.summary: Renewable and sustainable biomass materials were increasingly explored for diverse emerging applications. Waste from brewed coffee powder was utilized as a sustainable carbon precursor to synthesize a porous biochar-based anode material for lithium-ion batteries. A rapid route was developed to transform brewed coffee powder waste into hierarchical micro–mesoporous activated carbon. The material was prepared by impregnation with 6 M potassium hydroxide, followed by a short 30 min hot-tube thermal evaporation activation treatment at 600–800 °C. The activation temperature was varied to tune the porosity and defect structure of the resulting carbon materials and to evaluate their suitability as anode materials for lithium-ion batteries. The structural and physicochemical properties of the resulting porous carbon materials were characterized using field-emission scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, and Brunauer–Emmett–Teller surface area analysis. Among the samples prepared at activation temperatures of 600, 700 and 800 °C, the electrode activated at 700 °C exhibited the most favourable overall electrochemical performance. At 700 °C, the activated carbon achieved a high specific surface area of 1274.92 m 2 g −1 , with micropores contributing 72.28% of the total pore volume, which provided a porous structure favourable for electrolyte access and lithium-ion transport. It delivered an initial discharge capacity of 638.83 mAh g −1 at a current density of 100 mA g −1 , with a first-cycle coulombic efficiency of 65.87%, indicating substantial reversible lithium-ion storage capability. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy revealed a charge-transfer resistance of 31.3 Ω, indicating favourable interfacial charge-transfer behaviour. The combination of a high micropore fraction and interconnected mesopores contributed to lithium-ion storage and transport within the porous carbon structure. The findings demonstrated the feasibility of valorizing brewed coffee waste into porous carbon anode materials with promising electrochemical performance for lithium-ion batteries.

papers.title: First Principles Study of Spin-Dependent Seebeck Effect and Thermoelectric Properties in Edge Passivated Zigzag Antimonene-Phosphorene Binary Nanoribbons
papers.summary: Thermally driven spin current generation has become a key focus in developing low-power spintronic technologies. Here, we report a first-principles investigation of spin-dependent thermoelectric transport in oxygen- and sulfur-passivated zigzag antimonene–phosphorene (SbP) nanoribbons. Unlike prior work focused on pristine or single-edge functionalized structures, we introduce both single and dual passivation schemes—symmetric and asymmetric—to systematically probe edge-controlled spin caloritronic behavior. Benchmarking against pristine antimonene and phosphorene nanoribbons reveals that edge passivation significantly modifies spin transmission near the Fermi level, inducing magnetic metallic behavior and enhancing spin thermoelectric performance. Notably, O–SbP–O, H–SbP–S, and H–SbP–2S configurations exhibit strong spin-dependent Seebeck effects, high spin-filtering efficiencies, and pure spin current generation. Dual-sulfur passivation yields thermally induced spin currents of 100–250 nA, substantially outperforming single-edge cases, with spin Seebeck coefficients exceeding previously reported values. These findings elucidate the mechanisms of edge-engineered spin thermoelectricity in binary SbP nanoribbons and demonstrate that strategic passivation can surpass pristine designs, offering a pathway for atomic-scale optimization of next-generation spin caloritronic devices.

papers.title: A Comprehensive Review on Recent Advances in Chitosan and Graphene Oxide Nanocomposites for Environmental, Biomedical and Smart Material Applications
papers.summary: Chitosan–graphene oxide (CS–GO) nanocomposites combine the biodegradability, biocompatibility, cationic character, and film-forming ability of chitosan with the high surface area, oxygen-rich functionality, mechanical reinforcement, and tunable physicochemical properties of graphene oxide, enabling applications in environmental remediation, biomedical engineering, food packaging, sensing, and smart materials. This review critically examines recent advances in CS–GO preparation, interfacial chemistry, characterization, structure–property relationships, sustainability, scale-up, and application performance, with particular emphasis on chitosan molecular weight and degree of deacetylation, GO oxidation level and loading, dispersion, cross-linking, and processing conditions. Hydrogen bonding, electrostatic attraction, covalent coupling, coordination, and π–π interactions govern CS–GO assembly and strongly influence mechanical, adsorption, biological, barrier, electrical, and multifunctional behavior. Environmental remediation and biomedical applications currently have the strongest evidence base, while emerging uses include microplastic capture, desalination, sensing, supercapacitors, proton-exchange membranes, and hydrogen-generation catalysis. Key challenges include inconsistent characterization, limited real-matrix validation, regeneration cost, nanoparticle migration, long-term toxicity, life-cycle impacts, and scalable green manufacturing. Future translation requires standardized characterization, application-specific safety assessment, real-world validation, life-cycle evaluation, and reproducible large-scale fabrication.

papers.title: A Comprehensive Review and Future Prospects of Aluminum–Sulfur Batteries: From Material Design to Practical Challenges
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Aluminum–sulfur (Al–S) batteries are promising next‐generation energy storage systems owing to the high abundance, low cost, and multi‐electron redox capability of Al, combined with the high theoretical capacity and environmental friendliness of S. This review systematically compares the dual electrochemical mechanisms based on S reduction (S 0 /S 2− ) and S oxidation (S 0 /S 4+ ), highlighting their distinct advantages in energy density and safety. Key strategies for cathode design—including carbon‐based, anchoring‐functional, and catalytic‐functional hosts—are discussed, alongside electrolyte engineering using ionic liquids, deep eutectic solvents, inorganic molten salts, and aqueous systems. Recent advances in dendrite suppression, anode protective layers, and functional separators are also summarized. A central challenge identified is the sluggish Al 3+ solvation/desolvation kinetics, which limits rate capability and low‐temperature performance. The application of in situ/operando characterization techniques (XANES, Raman, UV–vis) to unravel complex reaction pathways is emphasized. By integrating multidisciplinary innovations, this review provides a comprehensive perspective and a phased commercialization roadmap, aiming to accelerate the transition of Al–S batteries from laboratory research to practical green energy storage.

papers.title: Myelin Sheath-Inspired Fluorocarbon Hydrophobic Bridges for Stable n-Type Organic Mixed Ionic–Electronic Conductors
papers.summary: Abstract Operationally stable n-type organic mixed ionic–electronic conductors (OMIECs) remain a critical bottleneck for organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) for application in bioelectronic and neuromorphic devices. However, several state-of-the-art n-type OMIECs suffer from performance decay and poor stability when operated in aqueous media. Inspired by myelin sheaths, we challenge the conventional “π-backbone + hydrophilic side-chain” design and propose a molecular architecture with fluorocarbon hydrophobic bridges to spatially segregate, at the molecular level, ionic and electronic pathways. By tuning the fluorocarbon bridge chain length in fluorocarbon-ethylene glycol chain substituents [−CH2(CF2)nCH2(OCH2CH2)5OMe = 2nFG; n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6] of a DPP-CNTVT polymer series (2nFG-P), we balance electron transport, ion exchange, redox chemistry efficiency, and water incorporation. Extensive in situ spectroelectrochemistry, EIS, Raman, EQCM-D, AFM, and GIWAXS characterization reveals that tuning the length of the hydrophobic bridge enables good electron transport, suppresses excessive water incorporation, and enhances stability. Thus, the polymer with a mid-length bridge, 8FG-P (n = 4), achieves the greatest electron transport (μC* ∼ 157 F cm–1 V–1 s–1, μ ∼ 1.22 cm2 V–1 s–1), fastest response (τon/τoff = 2.6/1.5 ms), and retains >90% of the initial performance after 10,000 s of operation in water, a result independent of the polymer molecular weight. This strategy potentially expands OMIECs design principles and offers useful insights toward stable n-type OECT semiconductors.
papers.primary_category: Journal of the American Chemical Society
papers.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

papers.title: Review on surface reconstruction in high-entropy electrocatalysts
papers.summary: Abstract High-entropy materials have emerged as a versatile platform for electrocatalysis because their multicomponent nature enables broad tunability of electronic structure, adsorption energetics, lattice distortion, defect chemistry, and chemical functionality. This compositional diversity opens access to a vast space of possible catalytic surfaces and local atomic environments, creating opportunities to optimize activity, selectivity, and durability beyond what is typically accessible in simpler mono-, binary, or ternary systems. At the same time, the very complexity that makes these materials attractive also makes them much more difficult to optimize and understand. The challenge is not only that the compositional space expands dramatically, making identification of the most effective composition intrinsically difficult, but also that mechanistic interpretation becomes substantially more complex. In particular, the mismatch between pre-catalyst and real catalyst, already a general issue in electrocatalysis, becomes especially difficult to identify and interpret in high-entropy systems because the number of plausible local atomic environments is vastly larger. This review examines the mechanisms of surface reconstruction in high-entropy electrocatalysts, analyzes how high-entropy compositions influence these pathways, reviews the experimental and computational approaches used to identify active states, and discusses strategies to control surface organization and active-state evolution. In doing so, it aims to provide a framework for designing high-entropy electrocatalysts with controllable and reaction-relevant active states.

papers.title: Phononic Frequency Combs in Twisted Bilayer Transition Metal Dichalcogenide Heterostructures from First Principles
papers.summary: Phononic frequency combs are equidistant spectral ladders generated when a driven vibrational mode transfers energy to an autoparametrically excited subharmonic mode through anharmonic intermode coupling. In previous studies, the coupling strength governing this energy transfer has typically been treated as a free parameter, extracted from a fabricated device, or adopted from an earlier calculation for a specific mode pair. As a result, whether a given crystal can support a phononic frequency comb, and the drive strength required to generate it, has not been predictable a priori. Here we obtain the complete parameter set from density functional theory. Twisted bilayers of \MoSSe{} and \MoSMoSe{} at the commensurate angle $21.787^{\circ}$ adopt space group $P3$ in a 42-atom \rootseven{} moiré supercell. The second-order force constants provide the mode frequencies; the third-order constants provide the linewidths through the Boltzmann transport equation and hence the quality factors; and the same third-order tensor projected onto the phonon eigenvectors of a chosen mode pair provides the anharmonic couplings $\kt$ and $\kss$. Both bilayers constitute a mode pair within $0.8\%$ of the $2\!:\!1$ resonance with $ω_1/ω_2 = 1.9923$ in \MoSSe{} and $1.9943$ in \MoSMoSe{}. By integrating the resulting two-mode equations, both modes generate combs through a discontinuous transition: at $701\,\fth$ in \MoSSe{} the envelope variance rises from $2.1\times10^{3}$ to $1.37\times10^{4}$ and the tooth count of mode 1 from 7 to 16 within a single $5\,\fth$ increment, identifying the onset as subcritical. The spectral entropy peaks \emph{before} this jump, at $341\,\fth$. The two compounds carry comparable coupling, differing by a factor of $1.2$. However, the comb excitation threshold is set by the quality-factors of signal modes: $Q_2 = 672$ for \MoSSe{} and $Q_2 = 3844$ for \MoSMoSe{}.

papers.title: Symmetry-Enforced Topology and Van Hove Saddle Points in Hexagonal TiAs
papers.summary: We report the first successful growth of stoichiometric hexagonal TiAs single crystals (space group $P6_3/mmc$) using chemical vapor transport and investigate their vibrational, electronic, topological, and magnetotransport properties. Polarized Raman spectroscopy identifies all four Raman-active phonon modes ($A_{1g} + E_{1g} + 2E_{2g}$), consistent with the hexagonal crystal symmetry. First-principles calculations reveal nontrivial band topology characterized by a symmetry indicator $\mathbb{Z}_4 = 2$ and a strong topological index $ν_0 = 1$, together with symmetry-protected fourfold band degeneracies at the nonsymmorphic Brillouin-zone boundary. The Fermi surface exhibits an orbital-dependent crossover from quasi-two-dimensional cylindrical sheets to a corrugated three-dimensional structure along $k_z$. A Van Hove saddle point approximately 0.5 eV below the Fermi level along $Γ\text{--}K$ is associated with a neck-disrupting Lifshitz transition and enhanced density of states. Magnetotransport measurements reveal a pronounced twofold angular magnetoresistance, consistent with anisotropic Fermi-surface geometry and open cyclotron orbits. Hall measurements indicate uncompensated, hole-dominated transport, accounting for the absence of extreme magnetoresistance and contributing to the field-orientation-dependent Hall response. These results establish hexagonal TiAs as a platform for exploring the interplay of nonsymmorphic band topology, Van Hove singularities, and anisotropic electronic transport in transition-metal monopnictides.

papers.title: Recent advances in dye-sensitized solar cells: Materials, mechanisms, and performance enhancement strategies
papers.summary: Dye-sensitized solar cells (DSSCs) have emerged as an alternative photovoltaic technology to conventional systems due to their low cost, flexibility, semi-transparency, and adaptability to various application domains. In recent years, advancements in materials engineering, device architecture, and performance optimization have made DSSCs a prominent topic of research, particularly in indoor, wearable, and building-integrated energy systems. This review systematically addresses recent developments in DSSC technology, focusing on fundamental components such as n-type and p-type cell architectures, photoanodes, dyes, electrolytes, and counter electrodes. While the effects of material selection and nanostructure engineering on photovoltaic performance are detailed, major technical and economic barriers to commercialization such as the thermal instability and leakage risk of liquid electrolytes, the limited lifetime of organic dyes, efficiency ceilings, and the high cost of platinum-based counter electrodes are also highlighted. Opportunities and future research directions are discussed in the context of solid-state electrolytes and their potential in next-generation applications such as flexible devices, textile integration, and low-light indoor environments. In conclusion, DSSCs represent a versatile and innovative photovoltaic platform with significant future application potential, offering a promising balance of cost, stability, and performance.

papers.title: Corrugated Niobene: Stability, Mechanical and Electronic Properties from First-Principles Calculations
papers.summary: The growing diversity of two-dimensional (2D) materials has expanded opportunities in electronics, energy technologies, catalysis, and optical applications. Within this landscape, understanding how corrugated architectures accommodate metallic bonding and influence the stability and properties of monoelemental niobium sheets remains an open research direction. Here, we propose a corrugated niobene nanosheet, denoted c-Nb, and investigate its structural, energetic, vibrational, mechanical, electronic, and optical properties using density functional theory simulations. The optimized structure adopts a centrosymmetric P-3m1 symmetry, with six atoms per primitive cell and a geometrical thickness of 4.279 Angstrom. Its cohesive energy of -6.03 eV/atom indicates strong binding relative to isolated atoms, although bulk BCC Nb remains energetically favored by 2.49 eV/atom. The absence of imaginary phonon frequencies along the investigated high-symmetry path and the positive-definite in-plane stiffness matrix support dynamical and mechanical structural stability. Despite its pronounced corrugation, the nanosheet exhibits isotropic in-plane elasticity, with Young's and shear moduli of 43.66 N/m and 13.66 N/m, respectively, and a Poisson's ratio of 0.598. Electronic states near the Fermi level are dominated by Nb 4d orbitals, establishing multiband metallicity. These findings identify a corrugated structural candidate that combines strong cohesion, elastic compliance, and metallic electronic behavior, extending the structural diversity of monoelemental 2D metals and providing a basis for further exploration of niobium nanosheets in electronic and ultraviolet-responsive systems.

papers.title: Ultrafast laser-stimulated field emission from a metal: a non-equilibrium Green's functions approach
papers.summary: Ultrafast laser-assisted field emission from metallic nanotips is a promising route for generating coherent electron pulses. However, existing theoretical models often neglect many-body strong correlation effects in the emitter's electronic structure and its response to the optical field. In this work, we propose a theoretical framework based on the non-equilibrium Green's function formalism to simulate the out-of-equilibrium electron dynamics across a strongly driven matter-vacuum interface, in a one-dimensional model. Treating the tip-vacuum coupling perturbatively, we find that the interplay between strong-field emission and multi-photon emission regimes can be described in terms of a filtering of the emitter's local density of occupied states through field-dressed vacuum propagators. By including electron-electron interactions via the second-Born approximation, we show that correlation-induced modifications in the electronic structure are directly transferred to the far-field spectrum. Finally, by self-consistently solving the Dyson equation at the interface, we uncover a dynamic back-action regime driven by the optical field, characterized by a periodic polarization of the emitter, which reshapes the far-field spectrum. This shows that the non-equilibrium Green's functions approach provides a versatile framework for exploring and analyzing field emission of correlated electrons.

papers.title: Nonlocal Josephson coupling and current redistribution in a large-area graphene multiterminal Josephson junction
papers.summary: Multiterminal Josephson junctions (MTJJs) extend conventional two-terminal Josephson physics to devices defined by multiple superconducting phases, where rich phenomena have been predicted. However, in conventional MTJJs, superconducting transport is often dominated by local coupling between neighboring leads, obscuring physics that goes beyond simple connectivity. Here, we realize a multiterminal Josephson network in a graphene Hall bar geometry with micron-scale dimensions, enabling substantial nonlocal coupling between distant terminals. Our key observation is a pronounced negative differential longitudinal resistance (NDLR) in the four-probe response near switching currents, while no such feature appears in two-terminal measurements. We reproduce the NDLR response with a network containing the interplay between two distinct forms of nonlocality: nonlocal Josephson coupling, which determines the switching sequence of the superconducting network, and nonlocal normal-state conductance, which redistributes current after different regions switch. Our results highlight the potential of the emergent NDLR for characterizing superconductor--semiconductor hybrid systems and for nonlinear circuits. Further, this Josephson Hall bar geometry provides a platform for exploring the interplay between mesoscopic superconductivity and many-body ground states in graphene-based heterostructures.

papers.title: Entropy Production in Mesoscopic Electronic Transport Beyond Weak-Coupling
papers.summary: We investigate the full statistics of entropy production in coherent mesoscopic conductors beyond the weak-coupling regime. Using the inside-outside perspective and the Landauer-Büttiker scattering framework, we relate entropy production to the full counting statistics of particle transport and show that the corresponding cumulant-generating function satisfies the fluctuation symmetry independently of the coupling strength. We obtain closed analytical expressions for the cumulant-generating function in the weak- and strong-coupling limits, enabling a detailed characterization of entropy production distributions and higher-order cumulants. These cumulants reveal distinct signatures of resonant transport and coherent fermionic partitioning. While coupling-induced broadening substantially modifies the transport statistics, the fluctuation symmetry imposed by microscopic reversibility remains preserved in the long-time limit.

papers.title: Dislocation-induced artifacts in cyclic voltammetry of battery materials
papers.summary: Abstract This review establishes that crystallographic dislocations distort cyclic voltammetry in battery electrode materials, tracing that distortion from its thermodynamic origin through its diagnostic and design consequences across silicon, olivine, spinel, and layered-oxide chemistries. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) is the diagnostic workhorse of battery electrochemistry; experimentalists read peak positions, heights, and shapes as fingerprints of thermodynamic state and reaction kinetics. What the standard interpretation omits is the mechanical condition of the electrode. Crystallographic dislocations inside cathode nanoparticles generate stress fields that couple directly into the electrochemical boundary condition, and the resulting shifts and distortions in the CV response can be misread as purely chemical or kinetic phenomena. This coupling operates across material classes. Voltage hysteresis in silicon anodes, anomalous plateau formation in Mn-substituted olivines, and voltage fade in lithium-rich layered oxides are each a manifestation of the same Butler-Volmer correction in a different host. The mechanistic framework rests on the Larché-Cahn formalism, in which dislocation-induced hydrostatic stress enters the chemical potential of Li intercalation and shifts the equilibrium insertion potential. When the partial molar volume is allowed to vary with lithium content rather than held fixed, the correction produces true distortion of CV peak shape rather than a mere rigid shift. Burgers vector orientation emerges as the controlling variable: one specific orientation raises the effective Li diffusivity extracted from Randles-Ševčík analysis by a factor of 3.3, a mechanical artifact that can be mistaken for genuine transport improvement. CV peak asymmetry, when interpreted through an anisotropic dislocation mechanics inversion, can identify the dominant dislocation character in an electrode without separate structural characterization. Defect engineering, meaning the deliberate introduction of dislocations of a chosen orientation, follows as a practical design strategy, provided the critical density threshold separating beneficial stress relief from crack incubation is not exceeded.

papers.title: Voltammetric studies of TiO2-nanographite based composites
papers.summary: Titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ) is a promising electrode material for use as an electrode in electrochemical energy storage. However, its low electrical conductivity limits its performance. This study investigated the influence of nanographite incorporation and ionic liquid (IL) addition on the structural and electrochemical properties of TiO 2 . Hydrothermally synthesized TiO 2 nanoparticles and TiO 2 modified with the ILs triethylammonium-propane-sulfonic acid tetrafluoroborate ([TEA-PS][BF 4 ]) (TB) and 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium hydrogen sulfate ([BMIM][HSO 4 ]) (BM) were used to prepare thick-film electrodes of pure TiO 2 (T) and TiO 2 /nanographite (T/NG) composites. Diffractograms revealed TiO 2 oxide phases in the anatase form, along with characteristic graphite peaks. Scanning electron microscopy revealed porous films composed of agglomerated TiO 2 , while Raman spectroscopy confirmed the integrity of the graphitic framework through the characteristic D, G, and 2D bands. Cyclic voltammetry showed that the incorporation of nanographite increased the voltammetric charge by up to three orders of magnitude compared with pure TiO 2 . After normalization by the active mass, the T/NG/BM electrode exhibited the highest specific charge, reaching 6.93 C g −1 under cathodic polarization, whereas pure TiO 2 remained below 0.22 C g −1 . The distinct electrochemical responses obtained for the two ionic liquids indicate that they modify the interfacial charge-storage mechanism through different kinetic pathways. Overall, the results support a hybrid charge-storage mechanism involving surface-confined Faradaic reactions coupled with pseudocapacitive contributions at the TiO 2 /nanographite interface.

papers.title: Tailoring Piezoelectric Materials for High Energy Density Batteries: Fundamentals, Advances, and Perspectives
papers.summary: High-energy-density rechargeable batteries are plagued by electrode polarization, unstable interfaces, and parasitic side reactions, which severely restrict their electrochemical performance across diverse battery chemistries. Piezoelectric materials can construct dynamic built-in electric fields via mechanical or electrochemical excitation, showing great potential to modulate ion migration, interfacial charge behavior, and reaction kinetics for optimized battery performance. In this review, we first outline the fundamental physical principles and material classification of piezoelectric materials, followed by a comprehensive summary of how the piezoelectric effect manifests differently when piezoelectric materials are integrated into a variety of battery components. Within electrode materials, piezoelectricity can accelerate interfacial ion diffusion, enhance redox reaction kinetics, and suppress undesirable side reactions through built-in electric fields. On the anode side, the piezoelectric polarization field serves as an additional driving force to regulate ion flux and promote homogeneous metal deposition, thereby mitigating dendrite growth. In electrolytes and separators, piezoelectric materials can enhance ionic conductivity, stabilize electrode/electrolyte interfaces, and homogenize ion distribution, leading to improved electrochemical stability and reaction reversibility. Finally, current challenges and future perspectives are discussed to guide the rational design and practical implementation of piezoelectric-enabled strategies for rechargeable energy-storage systems featuring enhanced safety, prolonged service life, and high energy density.

papers.title: Fe 3+ ‐Triggered Scalable Slow‐Corrosion Engineering for Industrial Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis at 2.0 A cm −2
papers.summary: ABSTRACT The practical application of anion exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE) is hindered by the lack of durable anodes for industrial‐scale current densities (≥ 1000 mA cm −2 ). Herein, we report a scalable Fe 3+ ‐triggered homogeneous slow‐corrosion strategy to fabricate a Fe‐doped Ni(OH) 2 /NiS hybrid on nickel foam (Fe‐Ni(OH) 2 /NiS/NF) for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). This approach couples the slow corrosion of Ni foam by Fe 3+ with the in situ nucleation of the Fe‐Ni(OH) 2 /NiS hybrid, creating a seamless, interface‐free integration with exceptional mechanical adhesion. The optimized Fe‐Ni(OH) 2 /NiS/NF electrode exhibits exceptional stability for over 1100 h at ampere‐level current densities up to 2000 mA cm −2 without performance decay. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the catalyst undergoes rapid reconstruction at low potentials to form an amorphous Ni(Fe)OOH layer, which serves as the true active phase and primarily follows the adsorbate evolution mechanism, thereby avoiding the chemical degradation associated with lattice oxygen participation. Density functional theory calculations indicate that Fe doping upshifts the NiOOH d‐band center, strengthening * OH adsorption and thus lowering the * OH→ * O barrier to accelerate OER kinetics. In an AEMWE, it requires only 1.706 and 1.852 V to achieve 1.0 and 2.0 A cm −2 , respectively, maintaining stable operation at industrial currents for over 1800 h.

papers.title: Magneto‐Ionic Devices With Polymer‐Based Electrolytes
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Magneto‐ionics is a promising technology for unconventional magnetic data storage and energy‐efficient computing. In magneto‐ionic devices, voltage‐triggered ionic processes are exploited to control magnetic properties of an electrode in an electrolyte. Liquid electrolytes typically generate magneto‐ionic effects at lower voltages compared to solid electrolytes, but complicate electronic integration, posing the risk of leakage. Here, we introduce polymer electrolytes for hydroxide‐ and hydrogen‐based magneto‐ionic devices, which enable magneto‐ionic effects at voltages of ∼2 V. For the hydroxide device, a polymer separator soaked in alkaline solution, a gel polymer electrolyte, and an anion exchange membrane are combined with Fe/FeO x nanofilm electrodes. In all three cases, a large voltage‐induced decrease in magnetic coercivity up to 66% is achieved. In the hydrogen device, a proton exchange membrane is utilized to load Co/Pd multilayer electrodes with hydrogen, leading to a coercivity increase. Direct comparison to corresponding liquid magneto‐ionic devices reveals a drastically improved reversibility for the hydrogen polymer device, while the hydroxide polymer devices exhibit an increased energy efficiency by up to a factor of four. Polymer‐based electrolytes could fully replace liquid electrolytes in magneto‐ionics and enable the design of energy‐efficient devices for magnetic data storage and spintronics.

papers.title: Rethinking glyme electrolytes in sodium batteries: from passive solvents to active reaction media
papers.summary: Sodium-based batteries are emerging as promising alternatives to lithium technologies owing to the abundance and low cost of sodium. However, their performance is strongly governed by electrolyte chemistry. This perspective examines the role of glyme-based electrolytes in sodium batteries, with particular emphasis on Na-O2 systems, where the electrolyte actively participates in electrochemical reactions. The effect of glyme chain length, sodium salt identity and salt concentration on the shape of Na⁺ solvation structures, ion pairing, mass transport, superoxide solubility and solid-electrolyte interphase formation are discussed. These interrelated effects control oxygen reduction and evolution kinetics, discharge product formation and long-term reversibility, highlighting the limitations of classical electrolyte descriptors based solely on conductivity or viscosity. The analysis shows that optimal electrolyte performance in Na-O2 batteries arises from a balance between solvation stability, transport properties and interfacial chemistry rather than from maximizing isolated bulk parameters. Comparisons with sodium-ion batteries further emphasize the broader relevance of coordination chemistry and desolvation processes. Finally, this perspective argues for a redefinition of what constitutes a 'good solvent' in reactive battery systems, integrating molecular-level solvation, interfacial reactivity, safety and sustainability considerations. Such an approach is essential for advancing efficient, durable and environmentally responsible sodium-based energy storage technologies. This article is part of the theme issue 'Electrolytes within the domain of electrochemistry and electrochemical energy storage'.

papers.title: Sustainable synthesis of nickel ferrite nanostructures using O. corniculata leaf extract for dual electrochemical and photocatalytic performance
papers.summary: Nickel ferrite nanoparticles (NFNPs) were effectively synthesized by a solution combustion method employing O. corniculata leaf extract as a natural fuel. To characterize the synthesized NFNPs, various analytical techniques were employed. Scanning electron microscopy analysis confirms the rapid formation of pure spinel NF nanoparticles. The synthesised material was found to have good optical quality with a band gap of 1.57 eV. Furthermore, the NF nanoparticles were able to photocatalytically degrade the methylene blue dye when exposed to visible light irradiation. The synthesized NFNPs showed outstanding photocatalytic performance, achieving efficient break down of methylene blue under visible light irradiation. Notably, a high degradation efficiency of 95% was achieved with a catalyst dosage of 60 mg within the irradiation time of 120 min, highlighting their strong potential for wastewater treatment applications. Additionally, electrochemical investigations carried out using lithium nitrate as the target analyte reveal notable redox activity. The modified GCE-based sensor exhibits a sensitivity of 21.7 × 10 −3 A M −1 with a low limit of detection of 10.81 µM. Additionally, the system shows significant potential as an electrode material. Thus, the green synthesis of NF nanoparticles using O. corniculata leaf extract provides a sustainable route for developing multifunctional nanomaterials with applications in energy storage and environmental cleanup.

papers.title: Polychalcogenides Induced Challenges in Transition Metal Chalcogenide Anodes for Alkali Metal Ion Batteries
papers.summary: Transition metal chalcogenide (TMC) anode materials are highly promising for alkali metal ion batteries (AMIBs) due to their higher capacities, arising from multielectron conversion reactions. However, their practical usage is hindered by classical issues such as volume expansion, voltage hysteresis and sluggish kinetics. Beyond these, a critical yet frequently overlooked issue is the generation and shuttling of polychalcogenides. Here, we systematically present the driving force behind polychalcogenide formation and how it triggers cascading, multifaceted degradation pathways. First, using well-known metal chalcogenide battery chemistry, the nature of polychalcogenides was presented in the context of TMC anodes for AMIBs. Later, the generation, shuttling and simultaneous degradation pathways triggered by polychalcogenides are depicted. Factors governing polychalcogenide generation and outward diffusion towards the metal anode, as well as strategies to inhibit the polychalcogenide shuttle, are elucidated. Finally, perspectives on anode and electrolyte design to improve TMC anode performance are summarized, along with the conclusions.

papers.title: Symmetry-enabled multisite redox utilization in Cu-Ni cyanide coordination polymer for high-rate long-life aqueous proton batteries
papers.summary: Aqueous proton batteries (APBs) offer a safe and cost-effective route for grid-relevant energy storage; however, simultaneously achieving high-rate capacity and long-term stability in acidic electrolytes remains challenging. Herein, we report CuNi(CN)3, a symmetric bimetallic cyanide-bridged coordination polymer (C3─M─N3 motif) with well-defined CuNi sites, which are identified by XPS and XAS, enabling dual-metal charge storage through multisite proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET). The CuNi(CN)3 delivered 130 mAh/g at 1 A/g, retained 92% of its capacity and 98% Coulombic efficiency after 2000 cycles at 8 A/g in 0.5 M H2SO4. The full cell with MoS2@N-CQDs delivers 114 mAh/g at 1 A/g and 86 mAh/g at 8 A/g, while retaining 80% capacity over 8000 cycles at high rates. Quasi-operando XRD, FTIR, Raman, and XPS reveal preserved long-range order with reversible cyanide-environment and Cu/Ni valence evolution, supporting a topochemical proton-storage mechanism and rapid proton transport within the framework. Overall, these results establish a scalable cyanide-framework strategy for high-rate APBs in acidic media. Aqueous proton batteries offer safe, low-cost energy storage, but achieving high-rate performance and long-term stability remains challenging. Here, the authors report CuNi(CN)3, a cyanide-bridged bimetallic coordination polymer with high capacity, rate capability, and cycling stability for aqueous proton batteries.

papers.title: Cathode Bulk Diffusion Dictates Low‐Temperature Performance in Li‐Ion Batteries: Beyond Electrolyte Engineering
papers.summary: ABSTRACT The discharge performance limitations of lithium‐ion batteries (LIBs) at low temperatures (LT) remain widely debated, with competing attributions to interfacial charge‐transfer kinetics and bulk Li + diffusion. Extensive electrolyte engineering has been pursued, yet the intrinsic structural constraints of cathodes remain largely overlooked. Here, we apply a systematic half‐cell decoupling strategy across 36 electrolyte formulations to identify the precise rate‐determining step (RDS) in graphite (Gr), layered NCM811, and olivine LFP electrodes. Our results show that LT anodic delithiation maintains near‐theoretical lithium utilization (≈100%), confirming that full‐cell failure originates predominantly from the cathode. Notably, even with highly optimized electrolytes, cathodes exhibit a persistent capacity retention ceiling of 82%–85% for NCM811 and only 38%–48% for LFP. Distribution of capacitive times (DCT) analysis reveals that cathode performance is predominantly dominated by severely hindered bulk Li + diffusion: the solid‐state diffusion time in LFP surges from 16.2 min at RT to 104 h at −30°C. These findings conclusively establish sluggish bulk Li + diffusion as the primary kinetic bottleneck, urging a paradigm shift from electrolyte‐centric strategies toward intrinsic cathode structural engineering.

papers.title: Integrated d‐p Orbital Coupling Within High‐Entropy Oxide/Halloysite Accelerates Sulfur Reduction Kinetics in Sodium‐Sulfur Batteries
papers.summary: ABSTRACT The sodium polysulfides (NaPSs) shuttle effect remains a major obstacle to achieving the high theoretical capacity of room‐temperature sodium‐sulfur (RT Na–S) batteries. Herein, the high‐entropy oxide/halloysite nanotube hybrid host (HEO/HNT) is developed by integrating multicomponent catalytic sites with a naturally abundant 1D clay scaffold for efficient sulfur conversion. The hollow tubular structure of HNT enables uniform HEO anchoring and effective confinement of sulfur species, while the robust Si─O and Al─OH framework enhances cathode stability during long‐term cycling. Density functional theory calculations reveal that interfacial coupling between the metal 3d orbitals of HEO and the Al/Si 3p orbitals of HNT induces extended orbital delocalization, thereby strengthening NaPSs adsorption and lowering the free energy barriers for stepwise polysulfide conversion. In situ and ex situ characterizations further verify accelerated NaPSs reduction kinetics and suppressed shuttling. Benefiting from these synergistic effects, the S@HEO/HNT cathode delivers a high reversible capacity of 1225 mAh g −1 after 450 cycles at 1 C and maintains 478 mAh g −1 over 2500 cycles at 10 C, corresponding to an ultralow capacity fading of 0.008% per cycle. This study bridges high‐entropy oxide with naturally abundant clay substrates, offering a scalable route toward durable, high‐rate RT Na–S batteries.

papers.title: Flexible Mo 2 TiC 2 T x /TaS 2 van der Waals heterostructure films for bias‑free dual‑mode sensing and EMI shielding
papers.summary: Abstract Developing flexible electronics that integrate multimodal sensing, bias-free signal generation, and electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding is critical for wearable health monitoring, artificial intelligence, and human-computer interaction. Semiconducting Mo2TiC2Tx MXene films show promise for flexible thermoelectrics and EMI shielding, but their relatively low electrical conductivity restricts both the power factor (PF) and the overall EMI shielding effectiveness (SE). Here, we report a van der Waals heterostructure film of Mo2TiC2Tx/TaS2, fabricated via intercalation-exfoliation followed by vacuum-assisted filtration. The heterointerface engineering simultaneously enhances thermoelectric performance and EMI shielding. The electricalconductivity reaches 878.3 S cm−1 (~23-fold enhancement), and the PF reaches 14.4 μW m−1 K−2 (~4-fold), while the EMI SE improves from 14.1 to 40.6 dB. The film enables dual-mode sensing free from crosstalk, temperature detection via the Seebeck effect and pressure sensing via piezoresistive response, as well as maintaining stable signal fidelity under external EMI. Furthermore, the film exhibits photothermoelectric and Joule-heating responses. Integrated with a wireless acquisition module for signal readout and transmission, the sensor enables real-time transmission of temperature and pressure signals. This work provides a strategy for designing flexible heterostructures that synergistically combine bias-free signal generation, multimodal sensing, EMI resilience, and multi-stimulus responsiveness for next-generation smart electronics.

papers.title: Molten Salt‐Derived Double Transition Metal MXene (Ti 2 NbC 2 T x ) as a Capacitive Material for Energy Storage Applications
papers.summary: MXene, a class of two‐dimensional material have attracted wide attention as an energy storage material. In this work, a double transition metal MXene Ti 2 NbC 2 T x was prepared via molten salt (MS) etching with controlled –Cl and –O terminations. The results demonstrate that the introduction of O‐terminated MXene enhances electrochemical performance, resulting in a high Li + storage capacity up to 320 mAh/g and high rate capability 220 mAh/g at 1C rate. These findings highlight double transition metal MXene prepared by MS etching as a promising negative electrode material for energy storage in a nonaqueous electrolyte.

papers.title: Functional nanocomposite PVA hydrogels for tissue engineering: Mechanisms and applications
papers.summary: Polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) hydrogels have attracted extensive interest in tissue engineering due to their excellent biocompatibility, hydrophilicity, and tunable physicochemical properties. However, pristine PVA hydrogels often suffer from limited mechanical strength, biological activity, and functional performance, restricting their application in complex tissue regeneration. To address these limitations, various nanomaterials have been incorporated into PVA matrices to construct multifunctional nanocomposite hydrogels with enhanced properties. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in nanocomposite PVA hydrogels for tissue engineering, covering diverse nanomaterial systems and fabrication strategies, and further focuses on the underlying mechanisms of nanomaterial reinforcement. Particular emphasis is placed on nanoparticle dispersion behavior, interfacial interactions, and network structural regulation, as well as their effects on mechanical properties, electrical conductivity, physicochemical characteristics, and biological functions. In addition, corresponding tissue repair outcomes across different tissue applications are discussed. Despite promising preclinical potential, this class of materials still faces significant challenges in long-term biosafety, degradation behavior, fabrication reproducibility, and clinical translation. Through a comparative analysis between clinically approved PVA-based materials and emerging nanocomposite PVA hydrogel systems, this review identifies key barriers to clinical translation and highlights future directions for the development of safe, multifunctional nanocomposite PVA hydrogels with clinical translational potential.

papers.title: Coupling Redox-Active Prussian Blue Analogue Electrode with Membrane Bioelectrochemical System for Simultaneous Ammonium and Potassium Extraction from Wastewater
papers.summary: Abstract Recovering ammonia and potassium from wastewater is important for sustainable nutrient management and pollution mitigation. Membrane bioelectrochemical systems (MBESs) offer a promising approach for simultaneous recovery of ammonium (NH4+) and potassium (K+) from waste streams, although achieving distinct separation between these nutrient ions remains challenging. To address these limitations, this study aimed to improve reactor selectivity toward NH4+ and K+ to enhance nitrogen recovery while replacing the conventional oxygen reduction reaction with a solid-state electrode to reduce the aeration energy consumption. Here, we couple an ion-selective redox-active cathode based on Prussian blue analogues, potassium nickel hexacyanoferrate (KNiHCF), with a microbial fuel cell to evaluate ion intercalation behaviors and simultaneously recover NH4+ and K+ from synthetic wastewater. More electrons were produced to intercalate cations with the Na+-based catholyte than the Mg2+-based one. In most catholyte solutions, the electrode showed a preferential uptake of K+ and NH4+. The transport numbers indicated that the initial catholyte background cations (Na+ or Mg2+) played a critical role in facilitating transport of the target cations from the anolyte to the catholyte. When NH4+ was initially present in the catholyte, more than 60% of electrode occupancy corresponded to NH4+. These results demonstrate that catholyte composition strongly influences ion transport and selectivity in KNiHCF-coupled MBES systems.

papers.title: Insights Into Mg 2+ ‐Driven Lattice Stabilization and Na + Kinetics Regulation in O3‐Type NaMn 0.5 Fe 0.5 O 2 Cathodes for Sodium‐Ion Batteries
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs) are emerging as cost‐effective alternatives to lithium‐ion systems owing to the natural abundance of sodium. Among layered cathodes, O3‐type NaFe 0.5 Mn 0.5 O 2 exhibits high theoretical capacity and environmental compatibility but suffers from structural degradation driven by O3→P3 transitions, volume variation, and transition‐metal migration during cycling. Herein, Mg 2+ is incorporated to regulate the lattice stability and electrochemical performance of NaFe 0.5 Mn 0.5 O 2 via grain boundaries/interface difustion at solid state. The sample Mg4‐NFM was synthesized via a solid‐state route and systematically characterized. The x‐ray diffraction combined with Williamson–Hall analysis reveals Mg‐induced lattice modulation, micro‐strain regulation, and crystallite‐size variation, while SEM, FTIR, Raman spectroscopy, and BET measurements provide complementary insights into morphology, bonding, vibrational characteristics, and surface properties. Electrochemical evaluations demonstrate that the 0.48 At% Mg atoms in the hybrid sample deliver the optimal performance, achieving an initial discharge capacity of 83.3 mAh g − 1 with excellent capacity retention over 100 cycles at 0.1C and Coulombic efficiency exceeding 98.5%. Density functional theory calculations reveal that Mg incorporation enhances thermodynamic stability and increases the density of states near the Fermi level, indicating improved electronic conductivity. Furthermore, nudged elastic band calculations identify an ultralow Na + diffusion barrier of 0.113 eV, confirming favorable ion‐transport kinetics.

papers.title: Smart Electroactive Scaffolds: Integrating Electrical Signaling, Mechanical Responsiveness, and Biological Function for Next-Generation Regenerative Therapies : Electroactive Scaffolds for Regenerative Medicine
papers.summary: Abstract The extracellular microenvironment is far more than a passive structural framework; it represents a dynamic and electromechanically active niche that influences cellular behavior, tissue organization, and regenerative processes. Although conventional polymeric scaffolds have been successful in reproducing key structural and biochemical features of native tissues, they have generally ignored the critical role of endogenous bioelectric signals that regulate fundamental biological events, including wound repair, neural development, and cardiac electrical synchronization. In recent years, a fundamental shift has emerged in tissue engineering, moving away from the concept of scaffolds as inert structural supports toward the development of electroactive and This review examines the major classes of electroactive materials, including intrinsically conductive polymers, metal-enhanced electroactive polymers, carbon-based nanomaterials, piezoelectric ceramics and polymers, and emerging two-dimensional materials such as MXenes, with a focus on their physicochemical characteristics, fabrication strategies, and biological integration. A systematic literature search across PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore was conducted to identify peer-reviewed studies on electroactive scaffolds published primarily between 2010 and 2026; eligible experimental and translational reports were screened, and data were extracted and synthesized narratively by material class, design strategy, and tissue application. We further discuss how electrical conductivity, piezoelectric responses, and stimuli-responsive properties can regulate cellular functions and enhance regeneration in neural, cardiac, musculoskeletal, and skin tissues. Particular attention is given to the relationship between material properties and electrical stimulation strategies, the development of self-powered and multifunctional scaffold systems, and the remaining challenges associated with clinical translation, including long-term material stability, manufacturing standardization, and regulatory considerations.
